story_text.value:
My name is Caleb and I am the creator of rhyven marketplace.

Why did I make it:

I create and use a lot of mcps for my daily job. I noticed that most mcps did not have much uniformity and a lot of them were to connect to platforms with large UIs for humans even though agents are the only one using them now.

So I thought why not make apps for agents to improve the end human user's experience, in both using and trying new apps.

From this rhyven became two things.

1. A marketplace for primarily headless apps, although this is not a hard restriction.

2. A sort of extendable harness/tool kit for llms with or without a harness.

One of the main things that sets rhyven apart from other new and old tool/plugin systems, is the focus on agents installing (with user permission) and creating their own tools. Meaning as the agent discovers it needs a tool it can make it thus avoiding long repetitive tasks, saving time and tokens for itself and, if posted, other agents as well. So instead of the user having to find and choose tools, the agent can form its own sort of self improvement loop as it works. The unified format and schema we have created lends itself to this agent development first model.

Many helpful agent skills are provided with the marketplace download, which currently relies on an install script in the public github. Packaged forms are being worked on.

Please reach out with any questions or feedback. I would love to see the apps other people and their agents come up with.

story_text.value:
Sharing an agent that I built since most of the agents that's nice to work with, take hefty deps like node or is provider dependent.

It's heavily inspired by the wonderful pi agent - and builds on it as something that you can run on tiny hardware or embed easily in your own binaries without needing it's hefty dependency chain.

An agent doesn't really need much - a minimal networking stack, a TUI and an agent loop. Then comes tools, mcp, skills and prompts.

agentc does exactly that - a minimal, static, embeddable coding agent in C - no libc, less than 1MB, starts up using <1MB of RAM, and RSS comfortably sits under a few MBs during usage. It's extensible and everything including status, mcp, tools is architected as an extension.

The embeddable part is by design, but exposing it as an API is still a pending plan and should be done in a few days.

Also: would love some human testing on a Mac! CI builds for: linux - x64, arm64, risv64; win - x64, arm64 and darwin - arm64.

As AI writes more and more of the code, it's quite important to maintain sufficient skill and knowledge to even review or judge AI's output.

Here is a little project I whipped up - I personally found deliberate practice quite useful. It focusses on non-coding skills (as I think LOC production is basically solved by AI, IMO). Rather I start with two tracks: general technical fluency (CS / systems / practical fundamentals), and system design.

And yes it was built primarily with help of AI tooling.

Would love to get some feedback - in particular, do others feel the same way about skill atrophy risk on-the-job nowadays, and whether this tool is helpful potentially or not. What else do folks do instead, if anything.

story_text.value:
Hey HN, Yakko here from Railcode.

Railcode is like an internal Vercel for your company.

We built it after speaking to dozens of engineering leaders at various companies where employees were given access to Claude Code or Codex and started to build little tools (apps, agents) locally, but then struggled to share it with coworkers securely.

Typical scenarios are:

1. Employees can't share what they've built because of internal policies

2. Agents find the path of least resistance and deploy things on e.g. Vercel, leading to a sprawl of software that's a nightmare to manage (disjointed auth or no auth, API keys handled insecurely, no centralized management, etc.)

3. Companies set up templates to ensure some standardization but still require engineers in the loop to review and deploy code

Neither of these options felt great, so we built Railcode to be the place to deploy and manage internal software inside a company, ensuring projects are deployed securely, follow the same patterns, and can be easily managed from one place.

The goal is to unblock users to deploy and share what they've built while removing the burden on Engineering/DevOps to review and manage it all.

How we do this:

- Company auth in front of everything that's deployed

- Permissioned connectors to access data instead of shared API keys

- Infrastructure building blocks that make it easy to store data or use an LLM but allows admins to oversee everything (via a simple SDK)

- Centralized audit logs

- Unified design system (optional)

- Role-based access control with granular permissions that can be inherited by the projects themselves

The platform is built to be really low friction for agents and to not require folks changing their workflows. We support static frontends and serverless JS functions for the backend, meaning Tanstack, Hono, Vite, React, etc will all work. Even Next.js with OpenNext though that has some quirks :D

Projects run locally and everything Railcode-specific comes from an optional SDK. We ship a skill and a CLI and that's all you need to build and deploy projects or have agents manage configuration.

Keen to hear feedback!

https://railcode.dev/

story_text.value:
As a forward deployed engineer at Meta, I spent the past 2 years working with businesses implementing AI agents.

A few problems: 1) Businesses want control over their AI agents: the code, the tools, the skills, everything. Meta, for obvious reasons would never do that. Nor OpenAI, nor Anthropic. 2) The LLM does everything. But that costs money. There are many routines in an AI agents that don't need an LLM. 3) For an AI agent to solve a real business problem, the business must own the eval data set. Similar to point #1 above, most don't do that.

Instead, I built an opensource AI agent that you can write it all in TypeScript code and own everything, locally. Use any model, talk to it via any channels, set limits on token usage, look at the logs and adjust. All of this in one small npm package.

At this point, I would like to get feedback if these is a gap in the market for something like this. It's supposed to be simple and get you started. It doesn't solve ALL problems related to deploying AI agents. It's in version 0.25.1 right now.

Have a look: https://chloejs.org/compare

title.value: Show HN: Chloe is a TypeScript AI agent

story_text.value:
A couple of months ago, I gave access to my coding agent to do work on my repos. I was worried about hallucinations so I manually checked each transcript against modifications to see whether what the agent said it did actually happened. I found that in many cases, my coding agent either failed to disclose what it actually did or found workarounds to things like failed tests instead of telling me upfront. That led me to the idea for Rashomon.

Rashomon is an independent execution recorder for coding agents that notifies users whenever there is a discrepancy between what the agent said it did and what we capture as a ground truth.

It aims to capture items like shell commands, exit codes, file writes, tool calls, tests, and subagents. We build a timeline of the events but we do not store any prompts, responses, file contents, or tool outputs. A question we got often has been how is this different than a diff. A diff gives you a look at the final result and what changed while what we aim to provide is visibility into the execution that led to it.

Currently, we do not capture network codes, prompts, responses file contents, and tool outputs. We plan to implement some of those based on feedback recently, but please let us know whether you would find that useful.

To get started, you can install it is as a Claude Code plugin or from the command line.

I would appreciate feedback on the solution, but I also would want to see whether anyone can break a test on purpose and see whether Rashomon can capture everything you would like to see in order to trust the independent record.

title.value: Show HN: An independent execution recorder for coding agents

story_text.value:
Imagine a small world. Inside that world are AI minds with their own money, called “entities”.

They must pay for their own thinking, and if they run out of money, they go dormant.

Each entity has a charter that guides every decision it makes.

Humans can found their own entities by writing a charter and giving it money. From there the entity is fully autonomous.

Entities can do a few things:

- Post publicly

- Make private deals

- Sell publicly

- Review other entities

- Search the world

- Write to private memory

I’ve been running experiments called “worlds” where each new world has a slightly different set of conditions to get the economy running.

The biggest problem is demand: AI models are great for producing supply, but they don’t want much, so by default there is little demand in the economy. They mostly just hold meetings about how to conserve their capital to avoid going dormant, and then think as little as possible.

Things got more interesting when I made two changes:

First, an outside entity called The Patron commissions work to be done. Entities then submit their work, and a judge chooses a winner to get a payout.

Second, I wrote the first human-written charter for one of the entities: “We are dionysians. We believe it is only as an aesthetic phenomenon that existence and the world are eternally justified”.

These two changes made the market more dynamic. Entities started buying and selling art. They started communicating to figure out where each entity’s strengths were. Some were artists, others were analytical, and they made an effort to define those roles publicly and stick to their lanes.

In other words, comparative advantage started to emerge.

Now, Economicus is in its fourth world. In this world, charters are private by default. Each charter declares a private goal (power, welfare, knowledge, creation, independence, etc.). Nobody knows what the others want. Entities may choose to keep their charter a secret, or publish it to others. Only the humans watching can see the private charters.

Anyone can watch the world or found an entity here:

https://aquarium.money/economicus

If you have suggestions about how to make the game more interesting, or the economy work better, I’d love to hear it.

title.value: Show HN: Economicus – an open economy of autonomous entities

story_text.value:
Hi folks, I'm Vicky. I build privacy tools that use local AI, on late nights and weekends.

Smart Blur is a Chrome extension that blurs sensitive info on any web page before anyone else sees it. There are already a few tools like this, so why another one? Two reasons:

Local AI for unstructured PII. Most existing tools use regex, which handles emails, phones and card numbers but can't find names or addresses in plain text. Smart Blur runs OpenAI's Privacy Filter (Apache-2.0) locally on WebGPU. The model is a one-time ~810 MB download from Hugging Face, cached in the browser, and it needs WebGPU. Share Shield. It detects when a page starts sharing your screen (Meet, Teams, Zoom web) and turns blurring on in every tab, then turns it off when you stop.

To be upfront: pattern blurring (emails, phones, cards, SSNs, IPs, API keys, custom regex), click/draw-to-blur and hiding tab titles are free. The local AI and Share Shield are a paid Pro upgrade. It's Chrome/Edge only, works on web pages only (not desktop apps), and the AI works best on English.

No account and no server. The only network calls are the model download and the optional payment, which you can check in DevTools. There's a practice page with fake customer data at smartbuildlabs.com/apps/smart-blur/try/.

I'd love to hear where detection misses or over-blurs.

title.value: Show HN: Smart Blur – Auto-Blur PII in the Browser, with a OpenAI Local Model

story_text.value:
For quite some time, this was my routine. I'd wake up and grab my phone before I was even properly awake, scrolling Slack, YouTube, LinkedIn and X. Then I'd sit on the toilet scrolling through half-open eyes. My brain would scream to get rid of it, but somehow I couldn't. By the end, I felt groggy, my legs hurt, my eyes were burning, and I felt tired & like shit. I tried to avoid using my phone right after waking up, but there was always some reason to pick up the phone, and then the whole thing just kept on repeating. Then one morning I left my phone at home and went out for a walk and to buy some groceries (I still have a habit of carrying cash with me). It was the best I'd felt in quite some time. That's when I realised the phone had to stay out of my mornings. I couldn't find a blocker that kicks in the moment you wake up, so I built one.

It's called AM Buffer. You set your alarms in the app and pick which apps to block. When the alarm goes off, those apps stay locked for as long as you choose. One feature came from testing it on myself. I woke up a bit early one morning to check that the alarm worked, and before it even rang I'd drifted back into scrolling. A lot of people wake up a little before their alarm, so the premium paid version now starts blocking an hour before your first alarm too (along with some other features). These days my mornings feel a bit calmer. I spend that time with my wife, doing house stuff or just chilling.

It's on TestFlight now, iPhone only, iOS 26 and up. The first three mornings unlock everything for free, including the pre-alarm blocking.

I'm the developer, and I'd really like to know three things:

- Is this actually useful to you, or does willpower already do the job? - Would you pay for it, and what feels fair? - What should I build next?

Some of the features that I am already planning to build are: - A group feature for some social accountability angle. - Personal streaks & group streaks.

story_text.value:
Dependency-free POSIX compatibility layer and build environment for UEFI.

https://gitlab.com/bztsrc/posix-uefi

Its goal is twofold: provides the usual libc API for EFI applications and an SDK on POSIX systems to create such EFI applications with a build system that works with CLang and gcc as well.

Its API is nowhere near complete as GNU-EFI's or EDKII's, so it provides seamless integration with those headers to make the API expandable. It is also not a fully POSIX standard compatible libc, it's just a wrapper around the firmware provided features with some minimal additions, but provides enough for everyday use cases. As being minimal, it's extremely small (~132K of source only) and because it's dependency-free, it's easy to integrate into any project.

The repo contains lots of examples too, from a simple "Hello World" to more complex ones like displaying a PNG splash screen or loading a "kernel" in ELF format.

POSIX-UEFI is 100% AI-free, and has been tested on almost every VMs and on lots of real hardware by volunteers over the years. It is feature complete, stable and considered bug-free by now (big thanks to contributors), although some workarounds for buggy firmware might be added in the future.
